rationale: Hunter, Definition 2.9, gives the same quantified definitions of lower bound, bounded below, and bounded (with the dual upper-bound notions). The item only specializes the ambient ordered set to the library's complete ordered field R and recalls the already-defined upper notions; it has no proof component.

Hunter, Definition 2.11, gives exactly the greatest-lower-bound definition: a lower bound greater than or equal to every other lower bound. The library adds only expanded quantifiers and uniqueness notation; the definition has no proof component.

Ernst's Theorem 5.42 identifies a maximum exactly with an attained supremum, and the surrounding definitions use the standard greatest/least-element convention. The item reformulates the standard notion as two standalone quantified definitions and appends the elementary uniqueness observation, so it is a semantic rather than cosmetic match; there is no proof component.

Hunter states uniqueness of both supremum and infimum and gives the same mutual-inequality proof: each supremum is below the other because the other is an upper bound, followed by antisymmetry; the infimum argument is dual. The library only expands this into numbered steps.

Hunter defines -A and states that m is a lower bound of A iff -m is an upper bound of -A, and later records the corresponding sup/inf reflection formulas. The library composes this standard duality with involutivity, nonemptiness, both bound directions, and boundedness consequences. The detailed positive-cone proof is locally supplied rather than followed from a displayed source proof.

Hunter states the same hypotheses, conclusion, and identity inf A = -sup(-A); MIT Theorem 38 gives the same reflected-set proof from the least-upper-bound property. The library faithfully expands that proof with uniqueness and order-reversal details.

Ernst's Theorem 5.43 and Hunter's Proposition 2.20 give the same upper-bound/epsilon characterization. The item adds explicit nonemptiness, boundedness, and complete-field existence hypotheses and phrases the comparison as u-epsilon, so the match is semantic. Its two-direction proof expands the source's immediate least-upper-bound argument.

Hunter's Proposition 2.20 gives the identical greatest-lower-bound characterization and the epsilon consequence x < inf A + epsilon. The library supplies explicit existence hypotheses and derives it through reflection and the supremum result, a sourced but materially reformulated proof.

Ernst's Theorem 5.42 states the same equivalence between a maximum and an existing attained supremum, with equality. The item splits the biconditional into two claims and adds an explicit nonempty ambient hypothesis; the direct proof is locally written from the definitions.

Hunter, Example 2.12, states that every nonempty finite set of reals has a greatest and a least element and that these are its supremum and infimum. The displayed list formulation is the same finite nonempty theorem, while the A4 repair materially replaced its stale statement-side Remark with a durable ordered-field observation; the resulting component is therefore a sourced but AI-altered presentation. The induction proof and forward listability bookkeeping remain local.

Hunter, Proposition 2.21, states sup A <= sup B under A subset B, using extended-real conventions. The library restricts to nonempty real subsets with a finite supremum and makes existence explicit. Its proof follows Hunter's upper-bound argument with the omitted existence checks expanded.

Olver, Lemma 2.16 and equation (2.8), state sup(A+b) = sup A+b and define the translate exactly. The library adds nonempty/bounded-above hypotheses so all suprema are real under its convention. Its epsilon-characterization proof is local rather than the source's singleton-sum deduction.

Hunter, Proposition 2.23, states positive scaling of suprema and negative scaling exchanging suprema with infima. The library separates the signs and makes the exact one-sided boundedness hypotheses explicit under finite-real conventions. The epsilon proofs for both signs are locally constructed rather than following Hunter's upper-bound division proof.

Hunter, Proposition 2.24, and Olver, Lemma 2.16, give the same Minkowski-sum identity. The library adds nonempty/bounded-above hypotheses appropriate to finite real suprema. Its proof follows Hunter's upper-bound plus two epsilon/2 approximations, expanded into the house proof format.

Hunter, Definition 2.15 and the surrounding discussion, gives exactly the extended-real values for empty and unbounded sets, says every real subset then has extended sup/inf, and warns that the extended line cannot be made a field because infinity-infinity and 0 times infinity are ambiguous. The item adapts that material into a house-convention remark; it has no proof component.

Hunter, Example 2.13, gives the exact construction (0,1), with supremum 1 outside the set, thereby refuting the exact claim that a bounded nonempty set's supremum must belong to it. The library's fully elementary epsilon refutation is local.

The sources state that least-upper-bound existence requires nonemptiness and boundedness and give empty/unbounded examples. The item combines the two independent failures into one false-statement construction, so it is a sourced composition rather than an exact reproduced statement. The two explicit refutations are local.
Hunter, Example 2.13, states exactly sup(0,1)=1 and inf(0,1)=0 with neither endpoint in the set. The guarded max/min epsilon witnesses and the attainment checks are a locally supplied verification.
Hunter's interval examples state that [0,1] has the same supremum 1 and infimum 0 as (0,1), with both bounds belonging to the closed interval. The direct maximum/minimum verification is local.
Hunter, Example 2.14, gives exactly the set {1/n:n in N}, supremum 1 attained, and infimum 0 not attained. The Archimedean epsilon verification and no-minimum argument are locally supplied.

MIT Theorems 27-28 use the exact rational set q>0, q^2<2 and prove it has no rational supremum; Hunter records the corresponding real supremum sqrt(2) and the density squeeze excluding a rational least upper bound. The item merges those established formulations and expands the density-based proof in the library's embedded-field notation.

Olver defines Minkowski sum, proves sup(A+B)=sup A+sup B, and derives translation of suprema; the example is the direct interval specialization (0,1)+(2,3)=(2,4). The exact numerical choice and midpoint decomposition proving reverse inclusion are local, but the construction is a recoverable specialization rather than a novel generated statement.

Hunter, Example 2.13, gives exactly the open interval counterexample with sup(0,1)=1 not in (0,1). This item packages that sourced construction as a counterexample and locally verifies the two-line consequence from the earlier example.

The sources use the natural numbers as the standard nonempty unbounded set with no supremum; Hunter explicitly records sup N=+infinity only under extended conventions, and MIT notes no ordinary supremum exists. The Archimedean proof in the complete ordered field is local.

Hunter states that the empty set is bounded above vacuously, explains why the least-upper-bound axiom requires nonemptiness, and assigns -infinity only after passing to extended-real conventions. This is exactly the construction recorded here. The explicit w-1 proof that no real upper bound is least is local.
